lessons.intro: You will learn how to find the core question hidden behind a messy problem. Starting with the right question saves hours of effort spent on the wrong answer.

cards.b: A complaint like sales are down describes a symptom. Ask what decision you actually need to make before you start gathering data.
Write the choice in one sentence, such as whether to cut prices or add a sales channel. A clear decision tells you which facts matter.
Ask why three times in a row to move from the surface issue to its cause. Each answer takes you closer to where effort will pay off.

fig.title: From symptom to decision
fig.note: Each why moves you one layer deeper.

ex.q: A shop's weekly sales fell 20 percent. Which question should be answered first?
o: How do we run more ads?
Why did sales fall, and which product lines dropped?
ex.why: Ads, hiring and closing are all possible solutions, so jumping to one is premature. First you need to know where and why the drop happened, which is the real question.

lessons.tip: Write the question down before you open a spreadsheet.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a symptom?
o: The root cause of a problem
An observable sign that something is wrong
A plan for the next quarter
quiz.why: A symptom is what you see, while the cause lies beneath it.

quiz.q: What is the first step when framing a problem?
o: Collect as much data as possible
State the decision you need to make
Ask a colleague for their opinion
quiz.why: A clear decision defines which information is relevant.

lessons.intro: You will learn to tell what you know apart from what you only believe. Mixing the two leads to confident decisions built on shaky ground.

cards.b: A fact is something you could verify with a record, measurement or observation. Customers paid 40 invoices last month is checkable, unlike customers prefer fast delivery.
An assumption is a belief you have not tested, often phrased as if it were obvious. Write each one down so it can be questioned before it drives a plan.
Label each statement as fact, assumption or guess. Anything in the last two groups becomes a question you must answer before committing money or time.

fig.title: Fact or assumption?
fig.note: Test every assumption before it shapes a plan.

ex.q: The till records show 70 of 100 sales happened at lunch. Which statement is an assumption?
o: Opening earlier will bring more customers
70 of those sales were at lunch
ex.why: The first, third and fourth statements are recorded or observable facts. Opening earlier will bring more customers is a prediction that still needs testing.

lessons.tip: Ask whether someone could check the statement against a record.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fact rather than an assumption?
o: Our website had 3,000 visits in May
Staff will adapt to the new system
quiz.why: A visit count can be checked against web analytics, while the others are predictions or opinions.

quiz.q: What should you do with an untested assumption?
o: Mark it and plan a test
quiz.why: Testing turns an assumption into a fact or shows it was wrong before it costs you.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to set a clear measure of success before working on a problem. Without one, you cannot tell whether your effort helped.

cards.b: Phrases like get better are impossible to judge. A measure such as raising repeat orders from 20 to 30 percent gives you a finish line.
Pick a single primary goal and at most two supporting measures. Too many targets pull effort in opposite directions.
Decide when you will review the result, such as after six weeks. A fixed date keeps the test honest and stops endless tinkering.

fig.title: Repeat order rate, percent
fig.note: Set the target before you see the result.

ex.q: A gym wants more members. Which goal is the most measurable?
ex.why: Gaining 40 members by March has a number and a date, so you can clearly tell whether it was reached. The other options are vague and cannot be checked.

lessons.tip: If you cannot measure success, you cannot prove you achieved it.

quiz.q: Why set a deadline for reviewing results?
o: It makes the report look official
It stops you changing the goal endlessly
It replaces the need for a measure
quiz.why: A fixed review date keeps the test honest and stops you moving the goalposts.

quiz.q: Which is the best primary measure for an online shop?
quiz.why: Monthly orders from new customers directly reflects growth and can be counted each month.

lessons.intro: You will learn to identify the limits that shape every decision, such as time, money and people. Knowing them early keeps your plan realistic.

cards.b: A constraint is something you cannot easily change, such as a budget cap, a legal rule or a deadline. List them before you consider options.
Hard constraints must be respected, while soft ones are preferences you could trade away. Knowing which is which opens up more choices.
Once the limits are clear, the problem often shrinks to a few real options. This focus stops you wasting effort on impossible plans.

fig.title: Finding the limits
fig.note: Work within the hard limits first.

ex.q: A team wants a new app. The launch must happen before a legal deadline in six weeks. Which is a hard constraint?
o: The team would like a blue logo
The launch must meet the legal deadline
Users might enjoy a dark mode
ex.why: A legal deadline cannot be negotiated away, so it limits your plan. The other options are preferences that could be traded.

lessons.tip: A constraint you ignore becomes a surprise later.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between hard and soft constraints?
o: Soft ones are preferences that can be traded
quiz.why: Soft constraints are flexible preferences, while hard ones must be respected.

quiz.q: Why list constraints before choosing options?
o: They remove options you cannot realistically pursue
quiz.why: Knowing the limits early removes impossible options and keeps effort focused.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to list everyone affected by a problem and what each one needs. Missing a key person can sink an otherwise good plan.

cards.b: Stakeholders include anyone who gains, loses, pays or makes the decision. Include quieter groups, such as the staff who will do the actual work.
Each stakeholder cares about something specific, such as cost, speed or risk. Writing these down shows where interests agree and where they clash.
Some people have the power to block a plan, while others care deeply but have little power. Give the most influential people early attention.

fig.title: Who needs most attention
fig.note: Top left needs the closest attention, so start there.

ex.q: A manager wants a new reporting tool. The finance director controls the budget and has not been consulted. What should the manager do first?
o: Ask the software team to decide
ex.why: The finance director has high influence over the budget, so bringing her in early avoids a blocked plan later. Waiting until launch risks a costly refusal.

lessons.tip: Ask who will be surprised by the decision and talk to them first.

quiz.q: Who counts as a stakeholder?
o: Anyone who gains, loses or decides
quiz.why: Stakeholders include all those affected by or able to influence the outcome.

quiz.q: A stakeholder with high influence but low interest needs what?
quiz.why: Such people can block a plan, so keeping them satisfied prevents trouble later.

lessons.t: Breaking a big problem into parts
lessons.intro: You will learn to split a large, tangled problem into smaller parts you can actually solve. Each part should be simple enough to test on its own.

cards.b: Split a problem by stages, parts of a system or groups of people. Natural boundaries make each piece easier to understand and owners easier to assign.
The pieces together should cover the whole problem without big gaps or overlaps. A missing part means your solution will fail at that point.
Tackle the piece that carries the most risk or uncertainty first. If it cannot work, you learn that before spending effort on the rest.

fig.title: Effort by part, in weeks
fig.note: The riskiest part should be tested early.

ex.q: A project has four parts done in sequence: research (2 weeks), design (3 weeks), build (5 weeks) and testing (2 weeks). What is the total time?
ex.why: Add the four durations: 2 plus 3 is 5, plus 5 is 10, plus 2 is 12 weeks. Checking the total helps you see whether the schedule fits the deadline.

lessons.tip: If a part is hard to describe, it probably needs splitting again.

quiz.q: Why start with the riskiest part?
o: It is the cheapest to finish
It shows early whether the plan can work
It must be done first by law
quiz.why: Discovering a fatal flaw early saves the time and money that would be spent on later parts.

quiz.q: A project splits into three parts that overlap heavily. What is the main problem?
quiz.why: Overlap means people duplicate work and nobody is clearly responsible for each piece.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find the single step that limits the whole system. Improving anything else first often wastes money with little visible gain.

cards.b: In any chain of steps, the slowest one determines how much the whole process can deliver. Speeding up other steps changes nothing until this one improves.
Look for where work piles up waiting for the next stage. A growing pile in front of one step shows where the constraint lives.
Once you improve the bottleneck, another step will become the new limit. Treat this as a cycle, not a single fix.

fig.title: Items per hour by stage
fig.note: Sewing sets the pace for the whole line.

ex.q: A bakery makes 30 loaves an hour at mixing, 12 at shaping and 25 at baking. What is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour?
ex.why: The line can only move as fast as its slowest stage, which is shaping at 12 loaves an hour. Speeding up mixing alone would not raise total output.

lessons.tip: Improving a step that is not the bottleneck is wasted effort.

quiz.q: A process has stages that can handle 40, 15 and 22 units an hour. What is the maximum output?
quiz.why: The whole process runs at the speed of its slowest stage, which is 15 units an hour.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a step is a bottleneck?
o: It has no work at all
Work piles up in front of it
quiz.why: A growing queue in front of a stage means work arrives faster than the stage can process it.

lessons.t: Choosing the right level of detail
lessons.intro: You will learn how much detail a problem deserves before you spend hours on it. Too little leaves you blind, and too much buries the decision.

cards.b: A small, reversible choice needs a quick look, while a large, costly one deserves careful analysis. Scale your effort to what is at stake.
Stop gathering data once more information is unlikely to change the choice. Perfect knowledge is rarely available and rarely needed.
A rough model that captures the main drivers is often enough to decide. Add precision only where the rough version shows real uncertainty.

fig.title: Quick check or deep dive?
fig.note: Let the cost of being wrong set your effort.

ex.q: A stapler for the team costs 15 pounds and is easy to return. How much analysis should it get?
ex.why: A cheap, reversible choice does not justify heavy analysis. The time spent researching would cost more than any likely mistake.

lessons.tip: Ask what it would cost to be wrong, then size your effort to that.

quiz.q: When is a deep analysis most justified?
o: Any choice made on a Monday
Choices your manager has already made
quiz.why: Serious consequences from a wrong decision make extra analysis worth its cost.

quiz.q: What does aiming for enough mean?
o: Stopping once more data would not change the choice
quiz.why: When extra information cannot alter the decision, further research adds cost without value.

lessons.intro: You will learn a short framework for turning a messy choice into a clear comparison. It keeps you honest when emotions or sunk costs pull you off track.

cards.b: Write down every realistic option, including doing nothing, before judging any of them. An option left out early can never win.
Choose three to five criteria, such as cost, speed and risk, and rate each option against all of them. Using the same yardstick keeps the comparison fair.
Money or time already spent should not decide the future. Compare only what each option will cost and deliver from today.

fig.title: Simple decision frame
fig.note: Score every option against the same criteria.

ex.q: Option A costs 500 pounds and gives 8 benefits. Option B costs 700 pounds and gives 10 benefits. Which gives better value per benefit?
o: Option A, at 62.5 pounds per benefit
Option B, at 70 pounds per benefit
Option B, because it costs more
ex.why: Divide cost by benefits: 500 divided by 8 is 62.5, and 700 divided by 10 is 70. Option A gives each benefit at a lower cost.

lessons.tip: Money already spent is gone whichever option you choose.

quiz.q: What does the decision frame do first?
quiz.why: Listing all realistic options first prevents a favourite from being chosen too early.

quiz.q: Which is a sunk cost?
o: Money spent on a project last year
The cost of a new supplier
The price of a future option
quiz.why: A sunk cost is already spent and cannot be recovered, so it should not steer future choices.

lessons.intro: You will learn to turn vague beliefs into specific questions you can answer. A testable question tells you exactly what evidence would change your mind.

cards.b: Change people will love the new menu into will at least 30 percent of regulars order the new dish within a month? A question points to what to measure.

cards.h: Know what would prove you wrong
cards.b: Decide in advance which result would make you abandon the idea. This guards against finding reasons to keep a favourite plan.
Try the smallest experiment that could answer the question, such as a one-week trial. Small tests reveal the truth before large bets.

fig.title: Testing an assumption
fig.note: Loop through the cycle with each new idea.

ex.q: A cafe assumes 50 customers will try a new drink on a trial day. Only 32 do. What is the best next step?
o: Assume the drink will sell anyway
Compare the result to the target of 50 and decide
Repeat the trial until 50 is reached
ex.why: Measuring 32 against the expected 50 shows the assumption was too high, so you can decide on real evidence. Repeating the trial until it looks better is biased.

lessons.tip: A good question names the number that would change your decision.

quiz.q: Which is a testable question?
o: Will repeat visits rise by 10 percent this quarter?
quiz.why: It names a measurable outcome and a timeframe, so the answer can be checked.

quiz.q: Why decide in advance what would prove you wrong?
o: To make the result look official
To stop yourself moving the goalposts
quiz.why: A pre-set threshold stops you rationalising away results you do not like.

lessons.intro: You will learn to generate a full set of options, not just the first two that come to mind. Better choices start with a wider view of what is possible.

cards.b: Doing nothing has costs too, such as lost sales or rising repairs. Listing it lets you compare real alternatives against the status quo.
Your first two ideas tend to be the most obvious rather than the best. Ask for three more, even if they seem unlikely.
Mix parts of different options to create a new one, such as a lower price with a smaller product. Hybrids often beat the originals.

fig.title: Growing the option list
fig.note: Include the status quo as one option.

ex.q: A printer breaks down. Which list of options is the most complete?
o: Buy a new printer, or do nothing
Repair it, replace it, rent one, or use a print shop
Ask a friend to print for you
ex.why: The second list covers repair, replacement, renting and outsourcing, which is a broader range than the others. A list with several different routes is more likely to contain the best answer.

lessons.tip: Aim for at least five options before you start ranking any.

quiz.q: Why include a do nothing option?
o: It is always the best choice
It shows the cost of standing still
It is required in every decision
quiz.why: Doing nothing has real consequences, and comparing against it shows what each change is worth.

quiz.q: What is a hybrid option?
o: A mix of parts from different options
A repeat of the first idea
The option chosen by most people
quiz.why: Combining strengths from several options can create a better fit than any single one.

lessons.intro: You will learn that choosing one option means giving up the next best one. Seeing the forgone alternative makes trade-offs visible and honest.

cards.b: Money, time and attention spent on one thing cannot be spent on another. The value of the best alternative you give up is the opportunity cost.
Compare the returns of each option, not just the price tag. An option that costs less may still lose out if it returns less value.
Hours you spend on a task are a real resource. Valuing your time at a fair rate often changes which option looks cheapest.

fig.title: Net value of each option
fig.note: Choosing A gives up B, the next best at 700.

ex.q: You can spend a Saturday earning 120 pounds at a part-time job, or 60 pounds from a hobby sale. What is the opportunity cost of choosing the hobby sale?
ex.why: The opportunity cost of the hobby sale is the best alternative you give up, which is the 120 pounds from the job. The hobby's 60 pounds is the gain, not the cost.

lessons.tip: Ask what you give up, not just what you pay.

quiz.q: What is opportunity cost?
o: The value of the best option you did not choose
quiz.why: It measures the best alternative you forgo, which is what the choice really costs.

quiz.q: Why include your own time in the comparison?
o: Time is never a real resource
It can change which option looks cheapest
quiz.why: Time has value, so counting it can reverse a decision that looked cheap on money alone.

lessons.intro: You will learn to add up the full cost of an option over its life, not just the first payment. Ongoing costs often outweigh the price you see at the start.

cards.b: The purchase price is only the entry fee. Add running costs such as fuel, maintenance, subscriptions and staff time for an honest total.
Convert everything to the same period, such as yearly cost, so options can be compared fairly. A monthly fee and a one-off payment are not directly comparable otherwise.
Setup charges, renewal rises and penalties for leaving early can add up. Read the full terms before you assume the lowest price is lowest overall.

fig.title: Three-year cost comparison
fig.note: Buy: 900 upfront plus 300 a year. Lease: 55 a month.

ex.q: A machine costs 900 pounds to buy, with 300 pounds a year in upkeep. Leasing costs 55 pounds a month. Over three years, which is cheaper and by how much?
ex.why: Buying totals 900 plus three times 300, which is 1,800 pounds. Leasing totals 55 times 36, which is 1,980 pounds, so buying is 180 pounds cheaper.

lessons.tip: Always convert costs to the same time period before comparing them.

quiz.q: A plan costs 20 pounds a month. Another costs 200 pounds a year. Which is cheaper per year?
o: The 20 pound monthly plan, at 240 a year
quiz.why: Twenty pounds a month is 240 pounds a year, which is more than 200, so the yearly plan is cheaper.

quiz.q: What is a common hidden cost?
quiz.why: Renewal rises and setup charges often appear after the first purchase and raise the true cost.

lessons.intro: You will learn to set the benefits of each option against its costs in a single view. A clear balance makes it easier to justify your choice to others.

cards.b: Estimate what each benefit is worth, such as time saved multiplied by hourly pay. Putting benefits in the same units as costs allows a direct comparison.
Net value is total benefit minus total cost. A positive figure means the option pays for itself, and a larger figure ranks it higher.
A benefit-to-cost ratio shows how much you get back per pound spent. It helps when budgets are tight and cash is limited.

fig.title: Net value in four steps
fig.note: A positive net value means the option pays back.

ex.q: An upgrade saves 40 hours a year at 25 pounds an hour and costs 700 pounds. What is the net value in the first year?
ex.why: The benefit is 40 hours times 25 pounds, which equals 1,000 pounds. Subtracting the 700 pound cost leaves a net value of 300 pounds.

lessons.tip: Count only the benefits you can realistically achieve, not the ones you hope for.

quiz.q: What is net value?
quiz.why: Net value subtracts what an option costs from what it returns, showing whether it pays.

quiz.q: What does a benefit-to-cost ratio of 2.5 mean?
o: You lose 2.5 pounds per pound spent
You gain 2.5 pounds of benefit per pound spent
The option costs 2.5 times its benefit
It takes 2.5 years to pay back
quiz.why: A ratio of 2.5 means every pound spent returns 2.5 pounds of benefit.

lessons.intro: You will learn to estimate how likely a bad outcome is and how severe it would be. Combining both lets you weigh risk sensibly rather than by gut feel.

cards.b: A risk with a small chance but a huge impact can matter more than a common, minor one. Multiply likelihood by severity to rank them.
Use past data or reference cases to set a rough probability, rather than guessing high or low. Even a rough percentage beats a vague word like unlikely.
Ask what would happen if the bad outcome arrived, and whether you could survive it. Options that keep you safe from ruin are often worth a small premium.

fig.title: Two risks compared
fig.note: Expected cost: 60 pounds versus 400 pounds a year.

ex.q: A risk has a 2 percent chance each year and would cost 20,000 pounds. What is its expected yearly cost?
ex.why: Expected cost is probability times impact: 2 percent of 20,000 is 0.02 times 20,000, which equals 400 pounds.

lessons.tip: A rare disaster can still outweigh a frequent nuisance.

quiz.q: What is the expected cost of a 10 percent chance of losing 500 pounds?
quiz.why: Ten percent of 500 is 0.1 times 500, which equals 50 pounds.

quiz.q: Why is a rough probability better than a vague word?
o: It allows a direct comparison of risks
It removes the need for judgement
quiz.why: Numbers can be compared and ranked, whereas words like unlikely mean different things to different people.

lessons.intro: You will learn to ask how easily you could undo a choice if it goes wrong. Reversible decisions can be made faster, while irreversible ones deserve more care.

cards.b: Some choices can be reversed cheaply, such as trying a new tool for a month. Others, like signing a long lease, lock you in for years.
If you can easily undo a decision, try it and learn from the outcome. Waiting for perfect information costs more than most small mistakes.
Irreversible choices need more evidence, a clearer cost ceiling and a backup plan. The inability to undo them raises the price of error.

fig.title: How carefully to decide
fig.note: Match your care to how hard the choice is to undo.

ex.q: Which decision deserves the most careful analysis?
o: Trying a free trial of a planner app
Testing a new email subject line
Signing a five-year lease on a shop
Choosing a colour for a poster
ex.why: A five-year lease is hard to undo and commits large sums, so it deserves extra scrutiny. The other options can be changed cheaply and quickly.

lessons.tip: A reversible decision is a cheap experiment, so run it.

quiz.q: What is a one-way door decision?
o: A choice that is easy to reverse
A choice that is hard or costly to undo
A decision made by one person
A decision made in a hurry
quiz.why: The term describes choices you cannot easily walk back through once taken.

quiz.q: Why should reversible choices be made faster?
o: Waiting costs more than the small mistakes they might cause
They need no thinking at all
quiz.why: Delay has its own cost, and when mistakes are easy to fix, speed usually wins.

lessons.intro: You will learn when a fast, good-enough answer beats a slow, perfect one. Choosing the right trade-off helps you deliver value at the right moment.

cards.b: Getting an answer early lets you capture opportunities and learn sooner. A late perfect answer may arrive after the window has closed.
Cutting corners often creates bugs, complaints or repairs that cost more later. Quality matters most where errors are expensive.
A draft for internal discussion needs less polish than a contract sent to a client. Decide the standard by who will rely on the output.

fig.title: Weeks of work by approach
fig.note: Fast work plus later fixes can equal careful work.

ex.q: A fast version takes 4 weeks and then needs 6 weeks of fixes. A careful version takes 10 weeks with no fixes. Which finishes first?
ex.why: The fast version needs 4 plus 6, which totals 10 weeks. That equals the careful version, though the fast version gives you a working draft sooner.

lessons.tip: Match the quality bar to the cost of an error, not to habit.

quiz.q: When is a good-enough answer most sensible?
o: When the window of opportunity is closing
When a contract is legally binding
When the audience is a regulator
quiz.why: A timely answer can capture an opportunity that a perfect one would miss.

quiz.q: What tends to make fast work expensive?
o: It creates rework that adds time later
quiz.why: Errors skipped early often return as fixes, which can erase the time saved.

lessons.t: Comparing short and long term outcomes
lessons.intro: You will learn to compare options across different time horizons. An option that wins this month can lose badly over five years.

cards.b: Check the result after one month, one year and five years. Options can rank differently depending on the timescale you choose.
A pound now is worth more than a pound later, because it can be invested or spent. Discounting brings future figures into present terms.
Cutting maintenance or training boosts this year's profit but raises future costs. Ask what the option quietly borrows from later years.

fig.title: Gain by year: cut versus invest
fig.note: Cutting wins early, but investing wins by year five.

ex.q: Option Cut gives +400 in year one and +100 by year five. Option Invest gives +100 in year one and +900 by year five. Which is better by year five, and by how much?
ex.why: By year five, Invest reaches 900 against Cut's 100, a gap of 800 in Invest's favour. Cut looked better only in year one.

lessons.tip: Always ask what happens after the first year, not just during it.

quiz.q: Why is a pound now worth more than a pound later?
o: It can be invested or spent sooner
quiz.why: Money in hand can earn a return or be used immediately, so it has a time value.

quiz.q: What does it mean to borrow from later years?
o: Taking a loan from the bank
Gaining now by costing more in the future
quiz.why: Short-term savings that increase future costs shift the bill onto later periods.

lessons.t: Planning for what you cannot control
lessons.intro: You will learn to account for uncertain factors such as demand, prices and weather. Building in margin for them keeps your plan from collapsing when conditions shift.

cards.b: Pick the two or three factors that would most change the result, such as demand or exchange rates. Ignoring them hides the real range of outcomes.
Calculate the outcome under optimistic and pessimistic values for each driver. A range shows how sensitive the decision is to being wrong.
Hold extra money or time to absorb a bad case without failing. A small buffer often matters more than a slightly higher forecast.

fig.title: Possible monthly profit
fig.note: Test the low case before trusting the middle.

ex.q: A plan earns 5,000 pounds if demand is high and loses 1,000 pounds if demand is low. Both outcomes are equally likely. What is the expected outcome?
ex.why: Add the two cases: 5,000 plus minus 1,000 gives 4,000, and dividing by two gives 2,000 pounds. Equal chances mean a simple average is a fair expectation.

lessons.tip: A forecast without a range is a single guess dressed up as certainty.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of testing best and worst cases?
o: To show how sensitive the decision is
quiz.why: A range reveals how much the decision depends on uncertain factors.

quiz.q: What does a buffer do?
o: It absorbs a bad case without failure
quiz.why: Spare money or time lets you survive a poor outcome rather than collapse under it.

lessons.intro: You will learn to justify your final choice in a few sentences that others can follow. A written rationale makes decisions easier to defend and review later.

cards.b: Write one sentence naming the option you picked and one giving the main reason. Two sentences force you to commit to a clear position.
Note the main alternative and the trade-off you accepted. Future readers can then judge whether the reasoning still holds.
Name the signal that would make you revisit the decision, such as cost passing a threshold. Review points keep choices honest as facts change.

fig.title: Writing a decision record
fig.note: Keep the record short enough to read in a minute.

ex.q: Which decision record is best?
o: We chose it because it felt right.
We chose Option B because it saves 2 hours a week, accepting a 300 pound higher cost. We will review it if costs exceed 2,000 pounds a year.
ex.why: It names the choice, the main reason, the trade-off accepted and a clear review trigger. The other records lack evidence or any way to check the decision later.

lessons.tip: A decision you cannot explain in two sentences is not yet clear.

quiz.q: Why record the trade-off you accepted?
o: Readers can judge whether the reasoning still holds
It is legally required in all cases
quiz.why: Knowing what was given up lets others test the logic when conditions change.

quiz.q: What is a good review trigger?
o: A specific measure crossing a set threshold
quiz.why: A measurable threshold tells you clearly when the decision needs revisiting.

lessons.intro: You will learn to trace what usually happens after an action, step by step. Seeing the chain of consequences stops you being surprised by obvious follow-ups.

cards.b: Write down what happens immediately after your action. This first effect is often the one everyone already expects.
Ask what that effect causes next, and then what follows from it. Two or three links usually reveal the consequences that matter.
Competitors, customers and staff will each respond to your move. Their reactions often change the chain more than the original action.

fig.title: Chain of consequences
fig.note: Each reaction starts a new round.

ex.q: A shop cuts its prices by 10 percent. Which is the most likely next step?
ex.why: Competitors often respond to price cuts, which is a common second-order effect. The other options are less likely or do not follow from a price change.

lessons.tip: After every action, ask: and then what happens?

quiz.q: What is a second-order effect?
quiz.why: Second-order effects follow from the initial effect and often surprise planners.

quiz.q: Why map reactions from others?
o: They can change the outcome more than your action
quiz.why: Other people's responses frequently reshape the result of your original move.

lessons.intro: You will learn to see effects that arrive one step later and are easy to miss. Planning for them turns surprises into expected outcomes.

cards.b: A first-order effect is the direct result, while second-order effects come from it. Ignoring the second kind is a common planning error.
A rule or reward changes what people do, sometimes in ways nobody wanted. Ask how a sensible person would game the new system.
Every change can touch something beyond its target, such as staff morale or supplier terms. List those spillovers before you commit.

fig.title: First order versus second order
fig.note: Second-order effects can reverse the first gain.

ex.q: A council adds a bonus for every car park ticket issued. What is the likely second-order effect?
o: Staff may issue tickets to drivers who do not need them
ex.why: Incentives change behaviour, so staff may hand out tickets to earn the bonus rather than to enforce the rules. The other options run against what a bonus would encourage.

lessons.tip: Every incentive you create is a behaviour you will get.

quiz.q: What is an unintended incentive?
o: A reward that behaves in an unplanned way
quiz.why: It is a reward that changes behaviour in ways its designers did not intend.

quiz.q: Why list side effects before committing?
o: So you can avoid all change
So spillover costs are seen early
quiz.why: Spotting spillovers early lets you adjust the plan before the costs arrive.

lessons.t: Playing out a sequence of moves
lessons.intro: You will learn to think through a short game of moves and countermoves before acting. Two or three rounds ahead is often enough to avoid a bad opening.

cards.b: For each option you consider, ask how the other side is likely to respond. A move that looks strong alone may be weak after their reply.
Assume the other party chooses the response that hurts you most, within reason. Planning against a sensible opponent is safer than hoping for a kind one.
Think at least three moves deep before deciding. Shallow thinking often wins the first round and loses the game.

fig.title: Two moves, two replies
fig.note: Adding value beats cutting when rivals ignore you.

ex.q: You cut prices and your rival matches the cut. Which best describes the result?
o: You gain share with no cost
Both lose margin and neither gains share
ex.why: When a rival matches a cut, market shares stay roughly the same while both sides earn less. Playing out one reply shows the cut may only reduce profit.

lessons.tip: Before you move, ask what you would do if you were them.

quiz.q: Why assume a sensible opponent?
o: It makes plans safer than hoping for good luck
quiz.why: Planning against a sensible reply protects you if the other side acts in its own interest.

quiz.q: How many moves ahead is often enough?
quiz.why: Three rounds catches most traps without drowning you in branches.

lessons.intro: You will learn how small, repeated gains or losses grow over time. Compounding is one of the most powerful and most underestimated forces in planning.

cards.b: When returns are reinvested, each period earns on the previous total as well as the original. Early periods carry the most long-run weight.
A 50 percent fall needs a 100 percent rise to recover. Protecting against large losses matters as much as chasing gains.
Divide 72 by the growth rate to estimate the years needed to double. At 6 percent, money doubles in about 12 years.

fig.title: Doubling time in years
fig.note: Rule of 72: divide 72 by the growth rate.

ex.q: Money grows at 8 percent a year with reinvestment. Roughly how many years does it take to double?
ex.why: Divide 72 by 8 to get 9 years. The rule is an estimate, but it is close enough for planning.

lessons.tip: Recovery from a big loss takes far longer than the loss itself.

quiz.q: A fall of 50 percent needs what gain to recover?
quiz.why: Half the value must double to return to the original, which is a 100 percent gain.

quiz.q: Using the rule of 72, roughly how long does it take to double at 4 percent?
quiz.why: 72 divided by 4 gives 18 years, which is the estimated doubling time.

lessons.intro: You will learn to notice the small indicators that often come before a bigger problem. Catching them early gives you more options and less cost.

cards.b: Leading indicators move before the outcome you care about, such as order cancellations before revenue falls. Track them alongside the final result.
Decide the level at which a signal triggers action, such as three late deliveries in a week. Predefined triggers prevent denial when things slip.
Small anomalies are easy to dismiss but often come before failure. Review a short list of signals regularly rather than only at year end.

fig.title: From signal to response
fig.note: A signal only helps if it triggers a response.

ex.q: A software team sees bug reports rising steadily for three weeks before a launch. What is the best response?
o: Ignore it, since launches always have bugs
Delay the report to next quarter
Investigate the cause before the launch date
ex.why: A steady rise is a leading indicator, so investigating before launch leaves time to fix the cause. Ignoring or hiding the signal makes the problem more costly later.

lessons.tip: A signal with no threshold is just noise you will ignore.

quiz.q: What is a leading indicator?
o: A figure that moves after the result
A measure that moves before the outcome
A total of all past results
quiz.why: Leading indicators give earlier warning than lagging results do.

quiz.q: Why set thresholds in advance?
o: To trigger action before denial sets in
quiz.why: Pre-set triggers force action when a signal crosses the line, rather than rationalising it away.

lessons.t: Planning for the next decision point
lessons.intro: You will learn to see a decision as one stage in a longer journey. Choices made now should keep your later options open rather than close them off.

cards.b: A choice that locks you in can remove paths you might want later. Prefer moves that keep several doors open when the future is uncertain.
Decide now when you will reassess and what new information you expect. A planned checkpoint turns a one-off choice into a managed process.
Commit a small amount first, then scale up once evidence arrives. Staged commitments limit the damage if the first assumption proves wrong.

fig.title: Staged commitment
fig.note: Scale up only after each stage succeeds.

ex.q: A firm can invest 100,000 pounds now in one go, or invest 10,000 pounds, review after six months and invest more only if it works. Which keeps more options open?
o: Invest 10,000 and review before committing more
ex.why: Staging keeps money uncommitted until evidence arrives, so the firm can change course. A single large commitment locks in the whole sum before anything is learned.

lessons.tip: Ask what you would still be able to do after this decision.

quiz.q: What is a staged commitment?
o: Committing a small amount, then scaling after evidence
Signing a contract for each stage
quiz.why: Staged commitments limit exposure by releasing resources as evidence supports them.

quiz.q: Why schedule a checkpoint in advance?
o: To turn one choice into a managed review
To prove the first choice right
quiz.why: A scheduled review makes sure new information is actually used rather than ignored.

lessons.intro: You will learn to predict how rivals will react to your strategy. Strong plans assume competitors have their own goals and will act on them.

cards.b: Rivals optimise for their own goals, such as market share, cash or reputation. Knowing their priority tells you which moves they will tolerate.
A rival with deep reserves can outlast a price war that would ruin a smaller firm. Compare resources before picking a fight.
Firms tend to repeat how they handled threats before. Past reactions are often the most reliable clue to future responses.

fig.title: Rival A versus Rival B
fig.note: Know their means and goals before choosing a fight.

ex.q: A small firm plans a price war against a rival with much larger cash reserves. What is the main risk?
o: The small firm gains customers at no cost
The rival will leave the market
The rival can outlast the price war
ex.why: A rival with deep reserves can keep cutting prices for longer, so the smaller firm may run out of money first. Assuming the rival will simply give up is a common planning mistake.

lessons.tip: Judge a rival by its resources, not by how confident it sounds.

quiz.q: Why check a rival's resources?
o: To judge which fights it can afford
quiz.why: A rival with more resources can sustain costly responses that others cannot.

quiz.q: What is often the best clue to future rival behaviour?
quiz.why: Firms tend to repeat patterns, so their history is a practical guide.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to design plans that can adapt when conditions change. Flexibility has a cost, but it can be worth paying when the future is unclear.

cards.b: An option gives you the right but not the duty to act. Paying a small fee for flexibility can beat committing blindly.
Build plans from parts you can swap or scale independently. Modular setups let you adjust one piece without rebuilding everything.
Extra flexibility often costs money or simplicity. Pay for it when the uncertainty is large enough to justify the premium.

fig.title: Flexibility versus cost
fig.note: Flexible plans cost more but adapt far better.

ex.q: A firm can buy a machine outright for 50,000 pounds, or lease one for 3,000 pounds a year with the right to end the lease after one year. Which is more flexible?
o: The lease with a one-year exit
ex.why: The lease lets the firm walk away after a year, so it keeps a choice the purchase removes. That right has real value, and it is exactly what the outright purchase gives up.

lessons.tip: Flexibility you never use still has a price, so pay for it only when uncertainty is high.

quiz.q: What does an option give you?
o: The right to act later without the duty
quiz.why: An option preserves choice without forcing you to act.

quiz.q: What makes modular designs useful?
o: They let you change one part without rebuilding all
quiz.why: Independent parts can be adjusted without disturbing the rest of the system.

lessons.intro: You will learn a pre-mortem technique: imagine the plan has failed and work out why. This surfaces risks that optimism usually hides.

cards.b: Picture the project failing badly a year from now, then write down the likely causes. Starting from failure makes people speak more freely about weak spots.
Group the causes you listed and estimate how likely each one is. Focus your planning and monitoring on the most probable and most damaging ones.
Each risk needs a named person who watches for it and can act. Unowned risks tend to be discussed endlessly and managed never.

fig.title: Running a pre-mortem
fig.note: Do this before the plan starts, not after.

ex.q: A team lists three possible causes of failure. Which should they plan for first?
o: The supplier might be a day late
The lead developer might leave mid project
ex.why: A likely and severe risk deserves attention first, so the lead developer leaving is the one to plan for. The other risks are trivial or minor by comparison.

lessons.tip: The best time to find a flaw is before anyone has built on it.

quiz.q: What is a pre-mortem?
o: Imagining failure to find causes in advance
A test of the final product
quiz.why: It starts from an imagined failure and works backwards to surface risks early.

quiz.q: Why assign an owner to each risk?
o: So someone watches and acts on it
quiz.why: Without a named owner, risks are discussed but nobody acts on them.

lessons.intro: You will learn to order tasks so that early steps make later ones easier and cheaper. Good sequencing turns a long to-do list into a logical path.

cards.b: Some tasks unlock others, such as agreeing a budget before hiring. Doing these first prevents costly rework and blocked work later.
Put tasks that reveal the most information early in the plan. Lessons learned early can change everything that follows.
Batching related tasks reduces switching costs and setup time. A sequence that clusters work often finishes sooner than a scattered one.

fig.title: Hours lost to task switching
fig.note: Grouping similar work cuts switching time sharply.

ex.q: A team has three tasks that must run one at a time: agree the budget (2 days), hire staff (5 days) and buy equipment (3 days). What is the minimum total time?
ex.why: The budget must come first, taking 2 days, then hiring and buying take 5 and 3 days. Adding them gives 10 days, which is the minimum when only one task runs at a time.

lessons.tip: Ask what each task unlocks before deciding what to do next.

quiz.q: What is an enabling task?
quiz.why: Enabling tasks must happen first because later work depends on them.

quiz.q: Why front-load learning?
o: It lets early lessons change later plans
It makes the schedule shorter by default
quiz.why: Information gathered early can redirect the rest of the plan at lower cost.

lessons.t: Building a long-range strategy review habit
lessons.intro: You will learn how to keep your strategic thinking alive by reviewing plans on a regular rhythm. Strategy fails quietly when nobody checks whether the assumptions still hold.

cards.b: Set a fixed date, such as every quarter, to revisit goals and assumptions. Regular reviews catch drift before it becomes a crisis.
Compare each assumption you wrote down with what has actually happened. Any that have broken should trigger a plan change, not a quiet shrug.
Record major decisions with reasons and review triggers, so future you can see why they were made. Logs turn experience into reusable judgement.

fig.title: Strategy review loop
fig.note: Repeat the loop each quarter, not once a year.

ex.q: Your plan assumed 500 customers a month. Actual numbers have been 320 for three months running. What is the best next step?
o: Recheck the assumption and adjust the plan
ex.why: A persistent gap between assumed and actual figures signals that the plan needs updating. Keeping it unchanged or waiting a year lets the error grow unnoticed.

lessons.tip: A strategy you never revisit is just a hope written down.

quiz.q: Why keep a decision log?
o: It fills space in the archive
It shows the reasons behind past choices
quiz.why: A record of reasons helps future decisions learn from past ones.

quiz.q: What should happen when a key assumption breaks?
quiz.why: A broken assumption means the basis of the plan has shifted, so the plan needs adjusting.
